#What signals are

A signal is a fact about a request, worked out before the request is routed. It gives you three things:

Signals out of the box, and your ownThe gateway works out facts such as "has images" or "which client sent it" for free. You can add your own, such as "support topic" or "how hard is this".
VisibilityEvery signal is stored with the request. You can filter, list and group your traffic by it.
RoutingYour conditional routing can read a signal, so you can send each request to the model that fits it.

Examples: send requests with images to a vision model, send Claude Code traffic to Sonnet, send billing questions to Haiku.

#Where signals come from

SourceCheck to useModel callCost
Your own, by rules (including request facts)Rule SignalNoNone
Your own, by a modelRequest ClassifierYes, on your own integrationTokens, billed by your provider

Out-of-the-box signals (Rule Signal)

A Rule Signal can read these facts as request.<fact>, for example "request.has_images": { "$eq": true }. They need no model call. True or false facts match only { "$eq": true } or { "$eq": false }. The string "true" does not match.

FactValue
request.has_images, request.has_files, request.has_audio, request.has_toolstrue or false
request.tool_count, request.turn_count, request.input_charsa number
request.wants_json, request.is_stream, request.reasoning_requestedtrue or false
request.request_typechat_completions, messages, responses or other
request.context_sizeshort, medium or long. Medium starts at 4,000 characters and long at 24,000.
request.client_agentclaude_code, codex, cursor, cline, portkey_sdk, openai_sdk, anthropic_sdk, langchain or other. This is matched from the User-Agent and is a best guess.

Your own signals

  • Rule Signal. You write rules. The first rule that matches gives the answer, and a default applies if none match. A rule can read headers, metadata, body fields, the URL path, the last user message, the system prompt and the request facts above.
  • Request Classifier. A model answers a question about the request. The answer is a value from your list, yes or no, or a score. It adds one model call before routing. The timeout is 1.5 seconds by default and 2.8 seconds at most. It is listed as a PRO guardrail.

#Set it up

Temporary UI

You create signals today with guardrail forms. This is not the final experience. The final UI has its own Signals pages, and a signal you build now may need to be re-created there, if we cannot migrate it for you.

Start hooks are a new interception point. A start hook runs at the very start of a request, before routing. Signals run there. Conditional routing runs after them, so it can read what they produced.

Request
→
Start hookssignals run
→
Conditional routing
→
Input guardrails
→
Model
→
Output guardrails
  1. Create a guardrail. In Guardrails, choose Create and pick Rule Signal or Request Classifier. Name your own signals with lowercase letters, digits and _ (up to 40 characters). The name cannot change later. Answer values use the same characters, and one : is allowed.
  2. Attach it as a start hook. Add the guardrail's slug to start_hooks in your config, or to the default start hooks of your workspace.
  3. Check it. Send a request and read hook_results.start_hooks in the response, or the guardrail results in Logs.
Rule Signal example
Signal: agent    Answer Type: Choices    Default Value: other
Rules: [
  { "query": { "headers.user-agent": { "$regex": "^claude-cli" } }, "then": "claude_code" },
  { "query": { "headers.user-agent": { "$regex": "cursor" } },      "then": "cursor" } ]
Request Classifier example
Model: @openai-prod/gpt-4o-mini    Classification Method: Chat Completions
Signal: support_topic    Answer Type: Choices    Default Value: other
Question: Which support topic is the customer asking about?
Values: [ { "value": "billing", "description": "invoices, charges, plan changes" },
          { "value": "login",   "description": "cannot sign in, password, 2FA" },
          { "value": "other" } ]
Looks At: Current Ask    Timeout (ms): 1500    On Failure: Defaults

Looks At chooses what the model sees, up to 15,000 characters: Current Ask (your last message and the end of the reply before it), Whole Task, Session Setup (the system prompt) or Model Input (every user message).

What a working signal looks like in hook_results:

JSON
"start_hooks": [ { "id": "<slug>", "checks": [ { "id": "portkey.rule",
  "data": { "signals": { "agent": { "values": [ { "value": "claude_code" } ], "source": "deterministic" } } } } ] } ]

source is deterministic (rule), classifier or default.

#See signals in your logs and analytics

Every signal and its value is stored with the request. You can use them in four places:

  • Filters. Filter the logs by a signal and its value.
  • Log list columns. Add a column for any signal to the log list.
  • Log details. Open a request to see the signals it carried.
  • Summary analytics. In the Analytics summary tab, group by a signal to see how your traffic splits across its values.

Each classifier call also appears as its own log row, so you can see what it cost.

#Route on signals

This is where signals pay off: your conditional routing can read them.

Temporary UI

You add start_hooks and conditions to the config JSON by hand today. The final UI will do this for you.

JSON
{
  "start_hooks": ["<has_images rule slug>", "<agent rule slug>", "<classifier slug>"],
  "strategy": {
    "mode": "conditional",
    "conditions": [
      { "query": { "signals.has_images": "yes" },                              "then": "vision" },
      { "query": { "signals.agent": "claude_code" },               "then": "sonnet" },
      { "query": { "signals.support_topic": { "$in": ["billing", "login"] } }, "then": "haiku" }
    ],
    "default": "sonnet"
  },
  "targets": [ "...your targets as usual..." ]
}
Signal typeHow to write the condition
Text"signals.agent": "claude_code", or { "$eq": ... }, { "$in": [...] }
Yes or no{ "$eq": "yes" }. These are the strings yes and no, including for rule signals built on request facts.
Numbers and scores{ "$gte": 4 }, { "$lt": 2 }, { "$eq": 3 }

Combine signals with $and and $or. Conditions run top to bottom, and the first match wins. Always keep a default target.

"Is not" matches a missing signal. $ne and $nin are also true when a signal did not run. Pair them with a positive condition.

#If something is wrong

A broken signal never fails a request. It produces no signal, and routing uses your default target. So read hook_results. When something is wrong, data.degraded names the reason:

ReasonMeaning and fix
invalid_parametersA field value is wrong. The message names it. Fix the guardrail.
timeoutThe classifier took longer than Timeout. Raise it (2,800 ms at most) or use a faster model.
classifier_errorThe model call failed. Check the integration slug and the model name.
rate_limitedThe provider refused the call because of rate limits.
invalid_outputThe model answered outside your list. Clarify the descriptions or add an other value.
span_timeoutAll signal checks together took more than 3 seconds. Use faster models or fewer classifier checks.
provider_exception, dispatch_unavailableAn internal error. Send the hook_results to us.

Signal missing? Check that the guardrail slug is in start_hooks, that the request is a POST with a JSON body to /v1/chat/completions, /v1/messages or /v1/responses, that you did not send x-portkey-signals-off: true, and that no guardrail start hook denied the request first.

#Good to know

  • Signals run only on chat completions, messages and responses requests. Embeddings, audio and other routes skip them.
  • Regular expressions are case-sensitive. Inline flags such as (?i) do not work. Write [Rr]efund.
  • Classifier checks share one model call when they use the same model and Looks At. The whole signal step ends after 3 seconds.
  • The classifier sends request text to the integration you chose. It sends only what Looks At selects.
  • Switching models loses provider prompt caching. If your conversations use it, routing between models costs the cached prefix.
